q-29834:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $-\frac{5}{2}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{5}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{5}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡|x|-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡K \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

q-104297:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)={e}^{x}$ and $v(x)=cos⁡x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}({e}^{x}cos⁡x)^{′} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =({e}^{x})^{′}\cdot cos⁡x+{e}^{x}\cdot (cos⁡x)^{′} \\  & =({e}^{x})(cos⁡x)+({e}^{x})(-sin⁡x) \\  & ={e}^{x}cos⁡x-{e}^{x}sin⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

q-48516:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)={e}^{x}$ and $v(x)=sin⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=cos⁡x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot cos⁡x+(sin⁡x)\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & ={{e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x)|}_{x=\pi } \\  & ={e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =-{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-{e}^{\pi }.$

q-70672:
The period of $y=cos⁡x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for any integer $n$ we have

$$
cos⁡x=cos⁡(x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=8$ into the right-hand-side gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡x=cos⁡(x+16\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $cos⁡x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3},$ then $cos⁡(x+16\pi )=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.$

q-103242:
The period of $y=cos⁡x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for an integer $n$ we have

$$
cos⁡x=cos⁡(x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=6$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡x=cos⁡(x+2\cdot 6\cdot \pi )=cos⁡(x+12\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $cos⁡x=-\frac{5}{8},$ then $cos⁡(x+12\pi )=-\frac{5}{8}.$

q-158059:
First, let's recall the graph of $y=cos⁡x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13933487/assets/2373daf4b5fd26f098bf90e998e2685db6a8b793e94ac9d80b08ea423cb535c0.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of $cos⁡x$ is $2\pi .$

- Our graph is symmetric over the $y$-axis. This means that $cos⁡x$ is an *even* function, and we have

$$
cos⁡(-x)=cos⁡x.
$$

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of $cos⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡(-x+18\pi ) & =cos⁡(-x+2\pi \cdot 9) \\  & =cos⁡(-x).\end{aligned}
$$

- Secondly, using the evenness of $cos⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡(-x) & =cos⁡x \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi cos⁡(-x+18\pi )-\frac{1}{2} & =\pi \cdot 0-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-31245:
Factoring out the constant $-2$ and calculating the resulting integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -2{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =-2\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-71900:
Factoring out the constant $\frac{1}{2}$ and calculating the resulting integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-113887:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{5}^{x}}{ln⁡5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-66139:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {3}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{3}^{x}}{ln⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-2277:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int (5{e}^{x}+{2}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =5\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x+\int {2}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{e}^{x}+\frac{{2}^{x}}{ln⁡2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-31252:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{e}^{x}-{3}^{x}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =2\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x-\int {3}^{x}\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{x}-\frac{{3}^{x}}{ln⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-47998:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=sin⁡x$ and $v(x)={x}^{2}.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(sin⁡x)^{′}\cdot {x}^{2}-sin⁡x\cdot ({x}^{2})^{′}}{({x}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}cos⁡x-2xsin⁡x}{{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{x(xcos⁡x-2sin⁡x)}{{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{xcos⁡x-2sin⁡x}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
